<reason>Both sides argued at a high level, and the debate narrowed cleanly. Side A's strongest route was the "slogan or self-harm" dilemma around the word "over," plus the geometry point that Africa has no rich neighbour and purchasing power cannot be decreed. Side B, however, handled that pressure more honestly than A handled B's: when pressed, B named actual teeth (differential export duties, the marginal megawatt to an industrial park, rail capital to a regional corridor, forgone customs revenue) and explicitly accepted the losses, which collapsed A's dilemma into an ordinary cost-benefit question rather than a trap. B then won that cost-benefit on the metric it had established from the opening: employment for a youth bulge. The decisive move was B's flip of A's own Botswana example — good governance, saved rents, decades of stability, and still one stone and high youth unemployment. A's only answer ("diversification is slow and hard") concedes that "invest the rents well" is not a jobs strategy, and A never supplied an alternative jobs mechanism beyond the hope that manufacturing will emerge from commodity strength, which is vulnerable to A's own "speculative" standard. B also correctly held the motion as written: it demotes raw-material dependence on distant markets, not manufactured exports, which blunted A's otherwise sharp Korea/Taiwan attack; A's endowment rebuttal ("neighbours buy what they don't produce") partly cuts for B's regional-manufacturing case. A does land real damage — the smuggling/farmgate cost of export duties went unanswered in B's closing, and A got the last word framing the concession about the market "needing to be built" — but that is a cost B priced rather than a burden B ignored. Execution costs also cut against A: its Rebuttal 2 was clipped for exceeding the cap, and its pressure questions leaned into mini-speech and included a loose "three speeches in" miscount. B built the cleaner comparative case: the enclave path is certainly unable to hire, so priority must shift.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's inversion of Botswana: A offered it as proof that commodity rents plus good governance suffice, and B turned it into the strongest evidence that honest rent management buys schools but not jobs ("diamonds don't hire"). A's reply that diversification is merely "slow and hard" tacitly conceded the point and left A's own employment mechanism unspecified for the rest of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
